scope: Provisional board-based judgements recorded before fresh engine searches or classifier output. Selection is fixed in broader-game-context.json. Unresolved does not mean tactic-free, and source-game continuations are not assumed optimal.

cases.judgement: Mirrored queen-pawn development. e3, Nf3 or a central plan do not by themselves constitute a forcing tactical win.
Bd6 challenges Bf4. Bxd6 can be recaptured by c7; the bishop contact is an ordinary exchange, not a free bishop. Further development and kingside space remain plans.
Opposite-side castling, a locked centre and pressure on Nc3. Nge2 and preparing e4 are coordination and pawn-break ideas; no independent forcing gain identified.
The e6 pawn is defended by Kf7, so the e-file rook does not win it for free. Knight improvement and pawn breaks are plausible; king proximity may change tactics and requires checking.
White is in knight check. The attacked b3 pawn is defended by a2; Nd2+ is not automatically a profitable fork. Assess the legal evasion rather than borrowing a future White attack.
Both kings are active. Rd5+ is available, while Ra3 pins b3 toward Ke3 and Nf3 attacks kingside pawns. Need concrete defences; checking or pin geometry alone does not establish the primary tactic.
London-style development after ...h6 and ...Bf5. Normal e3/c3/c4 plans; no demonstrated forcing material win.
Bc6 absolutely pins Nd7 to Ke8, but Bxd7 can be recaptured by the queen. The geometric pin and a possible Ne5 increase pressure; do not call it a winning pin without a concrete gain.
White needs king safety and coordination after the exchange sequence. Nf3 may hit Qh4; an attack on a queen which can retreat is not necessarily a fork or forced material win.
Black's queen on d3 and bishop on a6 create pressure around White's central pawns. White has an extra exchange but awkward pieces. Do not infer a root material tactic from that static advantage.
Two rooks versus rook and bishop with a closed centre. Activate rooks and create pawn targets; no immediate free bishop or forcing gain identified.
Active rook ending with bishop support and vulnerable pawns. Rook checks and invasions may matter, but neither a skewer nor a winning king attack is established by geometry alone.
Sicilian wing gambit after ...cxb4. a3 or development offers compensation and recovery; the captured gambit pawn is not a newly hanging piece.
White has central space for sacrificed pawns. Nb4 is defended along the f8-b4 bishop diagonal, and Nc2+ would meet Qxc2 while Qd1 remains. Do not invent a free knight or an unavoidable knight fork.

Bd6 is active and can exchange on e7, but Be7 is defended. Nb5-c7 attacks the rook without checking Kg8. Evaluate piece coordination and actual defensive resources before announcing a fork or trapped knight.
Advanced d6/e5 pawns and queen-bishop activity versus Nf4 and an advanced a-pawn. Capturing e6 may offer a bishop to f7 and change promotion threats; no forced sacrifice or root gain assumed.
Qxd6+ checks along d6-e5-f4-g3-h2. White must address the check; its passed e6 pawn cannot simply advance through it. A later mating sacrifice must not be attributed to the current evasion.

White is a queen and pawns down with an exposed king. Rook activity may delay defeat; isolated checks or captured pawns should not masquerade as a winning White tactic. No proof that all defences lose identically yet.
Early Dutch/fianchetto development. Central development and king safety, not an established tactical combination.
Bg5 relatively pins Nf6 toward Qd8. The black centre has supporting pawns, and cxd5 is an exchange. The pin may restrict play but is not yet a proved material-winning tactic.

...Nxe5 just captured White's knight. fxe5 recovers that knight in an exchange; it must not be labeled a newly hanging knight or independent 3.2-pawn win. Watch the subsequent central exchanges separately.
Same-colour bishops and blocked central pawns. Black's bishop is restricted by its pawns, but restriction is not a trapped-piece tactic unless it can be won. White can improve king and pawns.

White has potential d5/b5/e6 breakthrough routes. A capture on d5 gives check to Ke4, unlike some nearby king placements, so move order matters. Require concrete pawn-race analysis; no automatic zugzwang label.
